incidents.inputs: A new preflight script whose whole purpose is to read a project's incident register before delivery, and an outside workshop that had translated the kit's folder names into its own language.
incidents.error: The register path was hardcoded to source/quality/incidents.json. On that workshop the script announced 'this project has logged no incidents yet' over a register holding 109 of them, and its checklist silently dropped every lesson that workshop had already paid for.
incidents.why: Two defects stacked. The path was assumed rather than resolved, and — worse — a failure to READ the file was rendered with the same sentence as a file that was read and found empty. 'Nothing to do' and 'nothing seen' produce the same value, and only one of them is good news. The script reproduced, on its first outside run, the exact failure family it was built to catch.
incidents.generic: A tool that reads a project's data must resolve that path rather than assume it, and must never render 'could not read the input' with the same words as 'read the input, it was empty'. A check that reports all-clear when it simply failed to find its input is worse than no check at all.

incidents.inputs: A plain-text email draft for a real recipient, already composed and hard-wrapped, a few lines slightly over the target width.
incidents.error: Ran a script to rewrap it to 78 columns. The script treated each already-wrapped line as a paragraph, so it re-broke every one: orphan words, a hyphenated word split across two lines, and the two-line sign-off folded into one. Done again on a second draft in the same session before the pattern was recognised.
incidents.why: The rewrapper's input model was wrong and untested: it assumed unwrapped paragraphs and got wrapped lines. Reaching for a script felt cheaper than retyping, and the damage was only visible on reading the whole output, which the first run did not do.
incidents.generic: Compose a plain-text message at its final line width from the start. Never post-process the wrapping of prose that is already wrapped: the tool cannot see paragraphs, only lines, and it will break words and collapse structure.

incidents.inputs: A daily scheduled sweep whose own instructions name the Gmail connector as the only path to the work mailbox, and a machine with two Chrome profiles connected, one signed into the work account and one into the owner's personal account.
incidents.error: A funding sweep read the owner's personal mailbox instead of the work one it is scoped to.
incidents.why: A routine decommissioned on 2026-08-26 kept its instruction file on disk, unregistered but runnable. That file asserts 'There is no Gmail MCP connector' (false since the connector was added) and tells the agent to drive the owner's logged-in Chrome at /mail/u/0/, which resolves to whichever account is default in whichever profile it reaches. The playbook that supersedes it was updated correctly; the executable copy of the old instructions was not removed. FIRST DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG: this was initially attributed to a silent browser fallback inside the daily drain, on the strength of that task's description mentioning funding, without checking whether a task by the literal name existed. It did.

guard.where: the decommissioned file now opens with a hard stop; docs/failure-modes.md §4; memory two-gmail-accounts

incidents.generic: When a routine is retired, delete or cap its instruction file in the same change as the decision. A superseded playbook is a stale sentence; a superseded automation left on disk is a stale sentence something can still execute, and it will assert facts that were true when written. Also: a task's description is not its identity — check whether a routine by the literal name exists before attributing behaviour to a different one.

incidents.inputs: check-fleet.mjs, which answers how far behind the template each instance in a workspace is. The update-kit skill instructs the owner to run it from their own project, not from the template.
incidents.error: Run from anywhere but the template, every 'N template commit(s) behind' is wrong, and the closing alert fires on it. `const templateHead = await git(ROOT, ['rev-parse','HEAD'])` with ROOT = process.cwd() takes the CALLING repo's head as the template's, so `sha..templateHead` counts the project's own commits since it last synced. Reproduced here: run from the template, huguescharnallet is 12 behind and personal-paul up to date; run from huguescharnallet, the same scan says 189 behind and 'no template HEAD to compare' for the up-to-date one — the second symptom the report had not seen, since an instance whose sha is not in the caller's history cannot be ranged at all.

guard.where: scripts/test-check-fleet.mjs — the behind count must be identical run from the template and from a project; verified failing on the pre-fix script. The template is located by its origin, and an ungrounded figure is refused rather than printed.

incidents.generic: A script that compares against a reference must locate that reference, never assume it is where it was started. The failure is silent in the worst way: the number is plausible, it moves in the right direction as work accumulates, and it grows with the project's own activity — so the more an instance is worked, the more urgently it claims to be out of date.

incidents.inputs: The SessionStart hook that announces kit news, registered in .claude/settings.json, and check-fleet's second question: is this instance WIRED to tell its own owner anything?
incidents.error: An instance can report 'news: wired' while the mechanism has never once run. The hook's command is `node "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/scripts/kit-news.mjs" 2>/dev/null || true`, so on a machine with no node it fails silently and succeeds loudly. check-fleet reads the hook's presence in settings.json and calls that wired. An outside user ran a month of sessions this way and found it only when a diagnostic prompt made him install node.

guard.where: kit-news writes .git/kit-news-ran on every run before any early exit; check-fleet reports 'configured' and 'ran' as different answers, and says outright that the receipt only exists from 2026-08-31 so an absence proves nothing yet.

incidents.generic: This is the kit's own rule about safeguards, applied to the kit: a check that never fires leaves no trace, so its silence proves nothing. `2>/dev/null || true` on a notifier converts every failure into a positive claim. A tool that reports on a mechanism must test the mechanism, not read its configuration — the configuration is what someone intended, not what happens.

incidents.inputs: check-fleet.mjs reads each instance's working copy on disk — .kit-sync, .claude/settings.json — to answer whether it is wired and how far behind it is.
incidents.error: An outside user's scan reported that a project had neither the hook nor .kit-sync, and he wrote to say so. Both were on origin/main and had been for days; his local clone was 118 commits old. He caught it himself before acting, but the report he nearly acted on said a healthy repo needed repair.

guard.where: check-fleet prints each clone's lag against its own origin above every verdict drawn from it, and the template clone's own lag above the whole report; covered by a test.

incidents.generic: A tool that inspects a working copy is answering a question about a checkout, not about a project, and it must say which. Reporting 'NOT WIRED' from a stale clone is the silent-expiry family aimed at the maintainer: the sentence was true of what was on disk and false of the thing the reader cares about. State the age of the evidence next to the verdict drawn from it.
